Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp A sudden rise in Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz follows an increasing number of air strikes between the US and Iran, as both sides trade intensifying warning shots, bringing the region closer to a new all-out war, while a third US aircraft carrier arrives in the region. The US and Iran have conducted widening airstrikes in a fast-moving cycle of violence since Sunday, while Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two more oil tankers exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, bringing the total number of tankers that caught fire in the waterway since Sunday to six.
The US military launched new airstrikes on Iranian missile launchers across southern Iran on Sunday night after Iranian forces attacked a US base in Bahrain and fired missiles at tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, in a significant escalation across the region, as the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier has now arrived to join two other carrier strike groups in CENTCOM's operating region.
Iran carried out a drone attack on a radar at United States’ Al Riffa Air Base on Sunday following other attacks on US assets in Bahrain on the previous day, ramping up its warnings and as a show force against the US build-up in the region. Iran has also reportedly attacked tankers in Hormuz which usually triggers immediate US strikes on Iran’s coastal military infrastructure.
The US military then struck Iranian launchers in Bandar Lengeh and Sirik in southern Iran on Sunday night, targetting a wider area than the previous strike cycles and with a higher rate of fire by both sides.
Flight tracking portals registered a much larger US Air Force presence over the Persian Gulf in the region than in the previous weeks, just as the US is continuing its military build-up.
The IRGC said on Sunday that two tankers were trying to cross the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz under direct US military guidance when they allegedly encountered naval mines that "lit up the skies for hours", Iran's Tasnim news agency reported.
The IRGC described the actions as a response to what it called the "illegal US blockade" and violation of Iranian regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning oil companies again that the southern route of the waterway was mined.
Then on Monday, Iran’s Navy announced that a "violator" oil tanker caught fire after colliding with a sea mine in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz and was unable to move.
“Turning off tracking systems and unauthorised entry into prohibited and unsafe maritime areas exposes offending vessels to serious risks,” Iran’s Navy said in a statement.
It was not clear whether the tanker is one of six tankers reported by the IRGC to have caught fire, or if a separate incident occurred, and claims by the IRGC and the army about the number of tankers damaged and details of the explosions have not been independently confirmed.
However, the UK's Maritime Trade Operations Authority (UKMTO) issued a statement confirming that it had received reports of at least one incident in the early hours of Monday morning when an oil tanker was hit by "an unidentified projectile" while passing out of the Strait of Hormuz.
"The collision led to a fire in the engine room," the report said, adding that so far no casualties have been reported and all crew members are safe and that "the assessment of the damage and the extent of the environmental damage is currently unclear."
Oil prices rose on Monday following the large number of vessels incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier arrived in the CENTCOM area of operations in the region, joining the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush carrier strike groups, marking the first time since the Iraq war that the US has three carriers in the Middle East.
The US military is now completing a massive build-up of naval and air strike capabilities of approximately 19 US warships in the region, including the Red Sea, including guided missile destroyers and cruisers alongside other naval forces.
Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal quoted US intelligence analysts who assess in a low confidence estimate that Iran now has between 1,500 and 2,500 missiles in addition to new drones and short-range missiles, while Israeli military officials place Iran’s new capabilities at 1,500 ballistic missiles.
On 10 November, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) released a picture claiming to show the head of Iran’s armed forces and the IRGC Aerospace Force commander touring tunnels with missiles and launchers which they called a new underground “missile city.”
The Iranian regime has continued its threats against renewed US wide-scale attacks, with military officials telling Iranian Tabnak News on Sunday that "Iran's new offensive military doctrine means that the country will no longer be limited to calculated retaliation and will break the cycle of escalation," and threatening US bases in Europe too.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio lashed out at the “Shia clerics of Iran” on Sunday, stating that “every problem in the Middle East, every major problem in the Middle East – the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, the Shia militias that destabilize Iraq, the fighting elements that supported Assad and the destruction of Syria, Hizballah in Lebanon – everywhere you turn, there is one common denominator: the Shia clerics of Iran and their expansionist mentality.”
“This is an extraordinary historic danger and one that cannot be ignored,” Rubio warned.
As both sides appear to intensify their warning shots to build pressure and force concessions, the former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz said in a post on X that “the current situation in the Strait of Hormuz is inherently unstable and cannot be sustained indefinitely," and "that even if neither side wants a broader confrontation, the current dynamics are pushing both toward escalation.”
“As long as the United States maintains its naval blockade and attempts to push tankers in the southern shipping lane, Tehran will continue to regard these actions as acts of war," the Iran expert said, adding that "Iran is unlikely to accept this reality indefinitely. Instead, it will seek to raise the costs of the blockade through further attacks on tankers and potentially other targets, particularly if US military operations continue around Bandar Abbas," Citrinowicz said.
“There is a fundamental asymmetry between Washington and Tehran. The United States may believe it can maintain the blockade for an extended period, but Iran sees it as a direct threat to its economy, sovereignty, and national security. For the Iranian leadership, accepting the blockade without responding would amount to accepting a new strategic reality imposed by Washington. That is simply not how the regime in Tehran operates,” Citrinowicz concluded.
